hints: Start by thinking what the word ionisation tells you about electrons, is an electron being added or removed to make an ion?
Remember that definitions in this topic are very strict about state, so ask yourself why gas is specified rather than solid or solution.
Consider why the definition refers to one mole of atoms rather than just one atom, and what charge the ion formed will have.
walkthrough:
Picture what ionisation really means**
Imagine a single neutral atom in the gas phase, isolated from all its neighbours. First ionisation is simply pulling its outermost electron completely away to infinity, leaving a $1+$ ion: $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$. You are not removing a second electron, you are not adding one, just the very first removal.

Lock in the three essential details**
Cambridge always checks three things. One electron removed, not two. From each atom in one mole, so the energy is quoted per mole in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. And both atom and ion are gaseous, so there are no lattice or hydration energies interfering, it is the isolated atom only.

Put it together as a complete definition**
Combine those ideas into one precise sentence: the energy required when one electron is removed from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous $1+$ ions. Miss out gaseous or mole and you lose the mark, so learn it word perfect.

Final answer: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous $1+$ ions.
$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$

hints: Look at the shape of the bar chart, A is very high then B drops sharply, which position in the Periodic Table gives a peak like A?
Think about what happens to electron arrangement when you move from the end of one period to the start of the next period.
Recall the three factors that control ionisation energy and decide which two change most when a new shell is started.
walkthrough:
Read the pattern in the bars**
A is a very tall bar, then B collapses to a very low value. That tall bar is a noble gas at the end of a period, with a full stable shell. B is the very next element, the start of a new period like Na after Ne. So you are comparing removal from a full inner shell versus removal from a brand new outer shell.

Compare distance and shell**
In A the electron comes from a shell that is closer to the nucleus and already full. In B the outer electron is in the next principal quantum shell, for example $n=3$ after $n=2$. It is significantly further from the nucleus on average, so the electrostatic attraction is much weaker.

Add in shielding**
B has an extra complete inner shell of electrons between the nucleus and the outer electron compared to the outer electron of A. Those inner electrons repel the outer electron and shield it from the full nuclear charge. More shielding plus greater distance means much less net pull from the nucleus.

Link to the drop in energy**
Because the outer electron in B feels much less attraction to the nucleus, it is held far less tightly and is much easier to pull away. That is why far less energy is needed, giving the sharp fall from A to B.

Final answer: Element B has its outer electron removed from a higher energy level / new shell, further from the nucleus than in A.
There is more shielding by inner shells in B.
Therefore there is less attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron, so less energy is needed to remove it.

hints: Recall whether atoms generally get bigger or smaller as you move left to right across Period 3 from Na to Ar.
Count what happens to the number of protons in the nucleus from P to T, and where the new electrons are being placed.
Think about how a larger nuclear charge with similar shielding changes the pull on the outer shell and therefore the radius.
walkthrough:
Visualise the sketch**
Draw your bars or points falling from left to right, highest at P and lowest at T. It is a steady decrease across the five successive Period 3 elements. No peaks in the middle, just a clear downward trend.

Track protons and shells**
From P to T you are moving across the same period, so each step adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same principal shell, the $n=3$ shell. Shielding stays roughly constant because no new inner shell is added, the inner $n=1$ and $n=2$ electrons shield by almost the same amount each time.

Feel the stronger pull**
With more protons but the same shielding, the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons increases. Think of a stronger magnet pulling the same shell inward. The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons gets greater, the electron cloud is drawn closer, and the atomic radius shrinks from P to T.

Final answer: Sketch: bars / line decreasing steadily from P to T.
Across the period nuclear charge / number of protons increases and electrons are added to the same shell with similar shielding.
Greater attraction between nucleus and outer electrons pulls the shell in, so atomic radius decreases.
